en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Saṅghādisesa-kanda
6. The Second Training Rule on Receiving Food At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā was beautiful, pleasing to behold, and inspiring.
When people saw the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā in the dining hall, being lustful, they gave her the finest foods.
The bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā, feeling guilty, did not accept them.
A neighboring bhikkhunī said this to the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā:
“Noble lady, why do you not accept it?
“Because I am lustful, noble lady.
“But are you, noble lady, lustful?”
“I am not lustful, noble lady.
“What does it matter to you, noble lady, whether this man is lustful or not, since you yourself are not lustful?
Come now, noble lady, having received with your own hand whatever hard food or soft food this man gives you, eat it or consume it.”
Those bhikkhunīs who were few in desires... they complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can a bhikkhunī speak thus:
'What does this man do to you, noble lady, whether he be lustful or not, since you yourself are free from lust'?"
“Come now, noble lady, having received with your own hand whatever hard food or soft food this man gives you, eat it or consume it.
… [The Buddha said: “Is it true, monks, that a bhikkhunī speaks thus:
‘What can this man do for you, noble lady, whether he be lustful or free from lust, since you yourself are free from lust’?”
“Come now, noble lady, having received with your own hand whatever hard food or soft food this person gives you, eat it or consume it.
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked her... [as before]...
“How, monks, could a bhikkhunī speak thus:
‘What can this man do for you, noble lady, whether he is lustful or free from lust, since you yourself are free from lust?
Come now, noble lady, having received with your own hand whatever hard food or soft food this man gives you, eat it or consume it’?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence … [as before] … And thus, monks, should the nuns recite this training rule:
‘If any bhikkhunī should speak thus: “What can this man do to you, noble lady? He is lustful;’”’”
“Whether you are lustful or not, since you are free from lust, come, noble lady,
having received with your own hand whatever hard food or soft food this man gives you, eat it or consume it. This nun, too,
has committed an offense that is an immediate offense, involving expulsion, a *saṅghādisesa*.
"But whichever" means whichever such...
"nun" means... [as before].
... [as before] ... this is the nun intended in this context.
"She should speak thus":
"What can this man do to you, noble lady, whether he is lustful or not, since you yourself are free from lust?"

“If she urges her on, saying: ‘Come, noble lady, accept with your own hand whatever this person gives you, whether hard food or soft food, and eat or consume it,’ there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, at her word, she accepts [the food] thinking, ‘I will eat, I will consume,’ there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
For every mouthful, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
At the conclusion of the meal, there is an offense of saṅghādisesa. This also...
It is said with reference to the preceding [offenses].
"An offense of the first kind" means that one commits it simultaneously with the transgression of the objective basis, even without a formal admonition.
"Nissāraṇīya" means one is expelled from the Saṅgha. "Saṅghādisesa" [means that which remains with the Saṅgha].
... [as before] ... for that reason also it is called a *saṅghādisesa*.
If she urges him, saying, "Accept the water and the tooth-stick," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
By her word, if he accepts them with the thought, "I will chew it; I will eat it," there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one encourages a yakkha, a peta, a paṇḍaka, or a human in animal form who is lustful on one side, by saying “Eat this or consume this,” from their hand, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, at their word, one accepts it with the thought “I will eat it, I will consume it,” it is an offense of wrong-doing.
For every mouthful swallowed, it is an offense of wrong-doing.
At the conclusion of the meal, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If she receives water or a tooth-stick and dismisses him, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.
If, at her word, he receives [the food] thinking, "I will eat it, I will consume it," there is an offense of dukkaṭa.
There is no offense if she sends her away knowing that she is not lustful,
or if she sends her away thinking, "She will not accept [the gift] because she is angry."
If she dismisses [the donor] by saying, “I do not accept [this] out of lack of compassion for the family,” it is no offense for one who is insane or for one who is a first-time offender.
The sixth Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
